stem: Employees chat with a deployed model every day, and a manager assumes the model is learning from these conversations. How do training and inference differ for a deployed generative AI model?

choices.text: Each chat request is a small training step: the model updates its weights after every answer, so it gradually learns the company's facts from employees.
Inference happens only once when the model is deployed, and every chat request after that is training that permanently adds the conversation to the model.
Each chat request is inference: the model uses fixed learned weights to predict tokens, and its weights change only through a separate training or fine-tuning job.
Training and inference are two names for the same process, and the deployment type chosen in Foundry decides whether the conversations are remembered.

stem: A chat model answers the prompt "Write a short welcome message for new staff" with a full paragraph. At a basic level, how does a generative language model produce that paragraph?

choices.text: It predicts a probable next token from the prompt and the text so far, adds it to the sequence, and repeats until the response ends.
It finds the closest matching paragraph in a stored library of human-written messages and returns that text with a few words changed.
It sends the prompt to a web search engine, copies the top result into the reply and then trims it to fit the maximum output length.
It writes every word of the paragraph at the same moment from a fixed template and then sorts the words into grammatical order.

stem: An insurer wants a chat assistant to answer questions from its product terms, which legal staff update every week. Answers must reflect the latest version and point to the source section. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Fine-tune a language model on the product terms each quarter so the terms become part of the model's weights and need no further changes.
Write all of the product terms into the system message once and keep that system message unchanged for every conversation from then on.
Use retrieval augmented generation to search an index of the current terms and give the model the matching sections to cite.
Train a new large language model from scratch on the product terms so that it knows nothing except the insurer's own documents.

stem: A logistics company wants a language model to classify short delivery notes on handheld scanners in its warehouses, where the network is unreliable. The task is simple, and speed and low cost matter more than deep reasoning. Which type of model fits best?

choices.text: A small language model such as Phi-4, which handles common language tasks efficiently and can run on lower-end hardware or edge devices.
An embedding model such as text-embedding-3-large on its own, because embedding models generate the category label as a text reply.
An image generation model, because it can turn each delivery note into a picture that the scanner's camera classifies more quickly.
The largest available large language model, because only models with the most parameters can classify short text into fixed categories.

stem: An architect is comparing large language models (LLMs) with small language models (SLMs) in the Foundry model catalog. Which TWO statements correctly describe SLMs compared with LLMs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: SLMs are always multimodal, while LLMs are limited to text input and text output and cannot accept images in a prompt.
SLMs are usually more efficient and cost-effective, which suits apps where speed and cost matter more than the hardest reasoning tasks.
SLMs are the better choice for the most complex reasoning and long, detailed content generation because they focus on fewer topics.
SLMs can only be deployed through managed compute on dedicated virtual machines, while LLMs can only use pay-per-token deployments.
SLMs can run on lower-end hardware or edge devices, while LLMs generally need more computational resources to serve requests.

stem: A university builds a tutoring app that must solve multi-step physics and math problems and work through complex scheduling puzzles, where accuracy matters more than an instant reply. Which type of model is the best fit?

choices.text: An embedding model, because comparing the vector of each problem with stored solutions always produces the correct worked answer.
A text-to-speech model, because reading each problem aloud lets the app check every step before it gives the student a final answer.
An image generation model, because drawing a diagram of each problem lets the model calculate the result from the generated image.
A reasoning model, which spends more processing on the request and is strong at science, coding, math and complex problem solving.

stem: A field-service app lets technicians upload a photo of a damaged machine part together with the question "What is wrong with this part and how serious is it?" The app needs a written answer. Which model capability is required?

choices.text: A text-only small language model that reads the photo's file name and size to infer what kind of damage the part probably has.
A multimodal chat model that accepts both text and images as input and generates a natural language answer about the image.
A speech-to-text model that turns the technician's question into a transcript and then attaches the transcript to the photo file.
An image generation model that accepts a text prompt and produces a new picture of the machine part in its repaired condition.

stem: Before deploying anything, a developer shortlists two chat models in the Foundry model catalog and wants to compare their benchmark scores, read their license terms and check the input data types they support. Where is this information gathered for each model?

choices.text: In the model card in the model catalog, which has tabs such as Details, Benchmarks and License that describe the model before it is deployed.
In the chat playground, which shows a model's benchmark scores and license terms only after the model is deployed and sent its first prompt.
In the Azure pricing calculator, which lists each catalog model's benchmark scores, license terms and supported data types next to its price.
In Azure Monitor metrics for the Foundry resource, which record benchmark results and license terms for every model listed in the catalog.

stem: A legal firm is building a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) app: it must find contract passages by meaning and then write answers grounded in those passages. Which TWO model types does the solution need? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A speech-to-text model that transcribes each contract into audio segments, which the search index uses to rank passages by relevance.
A text-to-speech model that reads every retrieved passage aloud so the language model can understand it better before writing the answer.
An embedding model that converts contract passages and user questions into vectors so the app can retrieve passages by semantic similarity.
An image generation model that turns each contract page into an illustration so that the search index can store pictures instead of text.
A chat completion model that receives the question plus the retrieved passages and generates an answer grounded in that content.

stem: A team compares models for a streaming customer chat, where users must see the reply start appearing quickly. In the performance benchmarks shown in the Foundry portal, which metric best reflects this need?

choices.text: Estimated cost, which combines the input and output token prices using a fixed ratio of input to output tokens, where lower values are cheaper.
Attack success rate, which measures how often harmful prompts succeed in producing unsafe output, where lower values mean a safer model.
Quality index, which averages accuracy scores across public datasets for reasoning, knowledge, math and coding, where higher values are better.
Time to first token, which measures how long it takes for the first token of a streamed response to arrive, where lower values are better.

stem: A startup is deploying its first chat model in Microsoft Foundry. It has no data residency requirement, its traffic varies from day to day, and it wants the newest models in the most regions. Which deployment type is the recommended starting point?

choices.text: Regional Provisioned, which reserves dedicated throughput units in one region and bills for that capacity whether or not requests are being made.
Global Batch, which processes large sets of requests asynchronously at a lower cost and returns results later rather than in real time.
Developer, which bills per token for temporary deployments that exist only to evaluate fine-tuned models and come without an SLA.
Global Standard, which bills per token, can route requests to any Azure region, and usually gets new models first with the broadest coverage.

stem: A bank in Germany must ensure that prompts and responses for its chat model are processed only inside the EU data zone. Its traffic is moderate and varies through the day. Which deployment type meets this need most directly?

choices.text: Global Provisioned, because reserving dedicated throughput units restricts processing to the region where the bank created its resource.
Data Zone Standard, which bills per token and processes prompts and responses only within the Microsoft-specified data zone, such as the EU.
Global Batch, because asynchronous jobs are processed in the region where the input file is stored rather than routed to other regions.
Global Standard, because data stored at rest stays in the chosen geography, so inference processing in any Azure region still meets the rule.

stem: A ticketing platform runs a high, steady volume of model calls all day and needs consistently low latency for its production app. A colleague suggests a provisioned deployment. What is the main trade-off of this choice?

choices.text: Provisioned deployments only accept batch jobs, so the platform would trade real-time responses for lower cost and results returned later in the day.
The platform gets steadier latency, but provisioned deployments only support small language models, so it must switch to a less capable model.
The platform gets reserved throughput and steadier latency, but it pays for the reserved capacity whether or not requests are being made.
Provisioned deployments remove the content filters to reach lower latency, so the platform would trade built-in safety checks for faster replies.

stem: Every night an online store wants a model to label two million product reviews by topic. Nobody needs the results before the next morning, and lowering cost is the main goal. Which deployment type fits best?

choices.text: Global Batch, which processes large asynchronous jobs at a lower cost than standard deployments and returns the results later rather than right away.
Developer, which is designed for short-lived deployments used to evaluate fine-tuned models and is billed per token without an SLA.
Global Standard with a high temperature, because more random output lets the model label each review faster at a lower token count.
Global Provisioned, which reserves dedicated throughput units for the store so that every review is labeled with the lowest possible latency.

stem: A support team has thousands of high-quality example replies written in its house format. Including enough examples in every prompt makes requests long and costly, and the team wants a smaller model to follow the format consistently. The facts in replies rarely change. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Fine-tuning, because additional training on the example replies adjusts the model's weights to the format and reduces the examples each prompt needs.
Retrieval augmented generation, because retrieving example replies from an index at request time permanently changes how the model writes its answers.
Training a new language model from scratch only on the example replies, because a model built from those replies can only write in that format.
A higher temperature, because more random sampling lets the model discover the house format from a few examples instead of needing many of them.

stem: A product description generator often repeats the same sentence, such as "Perfect for everyday use", several times in one long description. Which request parameter is designed to reduce this repetition?

choices.text: A higher maximum output token limit, which gives the model room to finish its description so that it no longer needs to repeat earlier sentences.
A lower top_p value, which narrows sampling to only the most probable tokens and so prevents the model from returning to phrases it already used.
A positive frequency penalty, which penalizes tokens based on how often they already appear in the text so far and so discourages repeated lines.
A stop sequence set to "Perfect for everyday use", which lets the model write the phrase once and then continue writing the rest of the description.

stem: A developer sees a top_p setting next to temperature in the chat playground and sets it to 0.1. What does this parameter do?

choices.text: It tells the model to keep only the top 10% of the conversation history and drop the remaining earlier messages before it generates a reply.
It limits the next-token choice to the smallest set of most probable tokens whose combined probability reaches the top_p value, here the top 10%.
It sets the share of requests that the deployment processes with priority, so that one request in ten skips the queue during busy periods.
It caps the response at 10% of the model's context window, so the answer stops once it uses a tenth of the tokens that the model can process.

stem: A document summarizer returns summaries that stop mid-sentence, and each response reports a finish reason of "length". The source documents fit well within the model's context window. Which change addresses this?

choices.text: Add the word "length" as a stop sequence, so the model knows to keep writing until it has produced a summary of the requested length.
Lower the temperature, because cut-off sentences mean the model is choosing random tokens that end the response before the summary is complete.
Switch to an embedding model, because embedding models return complete summaries in a fixed-length vector instead of in a text reply.
Raise the maximum completion tokens setting, because the model stopped after reaching the output token limit set for the request.

stem: An app asks a model for a single product description and wants generation to end as soon as the model writes the marker "###", without that marker appearing in the returned text. Which configuration does this?

choices.text: Set "###" as a stop sequence, so the model stops generating further tokens there and the returned text does not include the stop sequence.
Set temperature to 0, because a deterministic model always stops generating when it reaches a heading marker such as "###" in its own output.
Set top_p to 0.1, because restricting the token choices to the most probable ones prevents the model from producing any characters like "###".
Add "###" to the end of the system message, so the model reads the marker as the last instruction and ends each reply when it repeats it.

stem: A developer is moving a feature to a reasoning model and reads about reasoning tokens. Which TWO statements about reasoning tokens are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Reasoning tokens appear in the message content that the model returns, so users can read the model's full internal thinking for every answer.
Reasoning tokens occupy space in the context window and count toward the output token limit set by max_completion_tokens.
Reasoning tokens are produced only during training, so a deployed reasoning model uses no extra tokens when it answers a request.
Reasoning tokens are stored on the server as the model's long-term memory and are reused automatically for every later user of the deployment.
Reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens, so a request can cost more even when the visible answer is short.

stem: A team's chat app uses a Global Standard deployment. After the team added a long policy document as grounding text to every request, the monthly cost rose sharply although the number of requests and the answer lengths stayed the same. What explains this?

choices.text: Grounding text is processed by a separate search service that bills for each document read, and that charge appears on the deployment.
Global Standard bills per hour for reserved capacity, and the extra text forced the service to reserve more capacity for the deployment.
Standard deployments bill per token for both the input and the output, so the added policy text increases the input tokens of every request.
Global Standard bills a fixed charge per request, and requests that carry grounding text are moved to a higher fixed charge category.

stem: A developer writes a small Python app that sends shelf photos stored on her laptop to a vision-enabled GPT model deployed in Microsoft Foundry. The photos are not hosted anywhere on the web. How should the app include each photo in the request?

choices.text: Paste the raw binary bytes of the file into the text part of the message so the model reads them as ordinary tokens
Attach the photo to the deployment's details page in the Foundry portal so that every later request includes it
Put the local file path, such as C:\photos\shelf.jpg, in the image URL field so the service opens the file directly
Read the file bytes, base64-encode them, and pass a data URL such as data:image/jpeg;base64,... as the image input

stem: A team stores product images in a storage account that has public network access disabled and a private endpoint in their virtual network. Their app, in the same virtual network, passes blob URLs to a vision-enabled model in Foundry, and the images are never processed. What should they do?

choices.text: Add a Foundry project connection to the storage account so that the deployed model can read private blob URLs on the next request
Set the image detail setting to high so the model retries the download with a full-resolution request against the private endpoint address
Send the image bytes as base64 data, because the service fetches image URLs from Microsoft-managed infrastructure outside the network
Peer the app's virtual network with the Foundry resource's network so the model can download the images through the existing private endpoint

stem: An online shop's product photos are already published on its public website, at addresses such as https://shop.example.com/img/lamp.jpg. A Python app must ask a vision-enabled model in Foundry to write a short description of each photo. What is the simplest way to include each photo in the request?

choices.text: Put the photo's public HTTPS address in the image part of the user message, next to the text part that asks for the description
Upload all the photos to the Foundry project's settings page once, so that every later request to the deployment can refer to them
Download every photo to the app server first, because a vision-enabled model accepts images only as base64 data, never as addresses
Paste the photo's address at the end of the text part, because the model follows any links it finds in the prompt and opens the image

stem: A maintenance app sends wide photos of whole machines to a vision-enabled model and asks for the serial number printed on a small label in one corner. The model often misreads the digits. Which change is most likely to improve accuracy?

choices.text: Rename each photo file to include the expected serial number, so the model can compare the digits it reads with the name of the file
Raise the maximum output tokens setting of the request, so the model has more room to describe every digit that it recognizes on the label
Raise the temperature setting of the request, so the model considers more possible readings of each digit before it settles on an answer
Send a closer or cropped photo in which the label fills more of the frame, so the printed text is larger, while keeping all of its digits visible

stem: A developer's app asks a vision-enabled chat model to write a detailed description of each uploaded photo. Many descriptions stop in the middle of a sentence, and the response shows finish_reason "length". What should the developer change?

choices.text: Lower the temperature setting, because a high temperature makes the model end its answers early once it becomes less certain
Raise the max_tokens or max_completion_tokens value in the request so the model has enough room to finish the description
Relax the content filter on the deployment, because a finish_reason of length means part of the answer was blocked as unsafe
Compress every uploaded image to a smaller file, because large images make the model stop answering once its input is full

stem: A study app lets students upload a screenshot of a bar chart from their textbook and get a plain-language explanation of what the chart shows and which trend stands out. Which approach in Foundry fits best?

choices.text: Turn the screenshot into a vector with an embedding model and show the student the closest matching chart that was stored earlier
Send the screenshot with an instruction such as "Explain this chart for a student" to a vision-enabled GPT model in Foundry
Send the instruction to an image generation model, which redraws the chart in a simpler style that the student can read more easily
Run optical character recognition on the screenshot and show the extracted labels and numbers to the student as the explanation

stem: A team lists possible uses for a vision-enabled GPT model deployed in Foundry. Based on the limitations Microsoft documents for these models, which TWO uses are poor fits? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Writing friendly catalog descriptions from photos of camping gear for an online shop
Summarizing a photographed whiteboard of English meeting notes as short bullet points
Reading the exact square of every piece from photos of chess games in progress
Suggesting short alternative text for photos published on a company web page
Interpreting CT scans from a hospital and suggesting a likely diagnosis to the patient

stem: An insurer's app sends photos of damaged cars to a vision-enabled model with the prompt "What is in this image?". The answers describe the street, houses and weather instead of the damage. What is the best way to improve the answers?

choices.text: Make the prompt task-specific, for example "Analyze this car photo for an auto insurance report, detailing all visible damage"
Send the same photo three times in one request, so the model gives the car more weight than the street in the background
Keep the short generic prompt and raise the temperature, so the model explores more parts of the picture in each answer
Set the image detail level to low, so the model ignores background objects and concentrates only on the largest vehicle

stem: A beginner writes a Responses API call to a vision-enabled model in Foundry and must ask one question about one photo. How should the input be structured?

choices.text: A system message that holds the photo, followed by a separate user message that holds only the text of the question
A single input_text part whose text contains the question followed by the public URL of the photo written in plain words
Two separate API requests, one sending the photo and one the question, which the service links by matching their IDs
One user message whose content list holds an input_text part with the question and an input_image part with the photo

stem: A facilities app uploads photos named like room-214-broken-window.jpg and asks a vision-enabled model "Which room is this, and what is broken?". The model describes the broken window correctly but says it can't tell the room. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: The base64 encoding removes the file name, so the app should switch to public URLs, which pass the file name to the model
The model doesn't process original file names or image metadata, so the app should add the room number to the text part
The detail level hides the file name, so the app should set it to high so that the file name is read along with the image
The model can't read text in photos at all, so the app should run a separate OCR service and then send its output instead

stem: A new developer has a vision-enabled GPT model deployed in a Foundry project. Before writing any code, she wants to check how the model answers questions about a few sample photos, then reuse the working setup in her app. What should she do?

choices.text: Open the deployment in the chat playground, attach a photo, ask questions, and then open the sample code that matches her settings
Open the Images playground, upload a photo, and generate a caption, which is then copied into her application code as a constant
Create a content filter for the deployment and upload the photos there, because filtering results show what the model would answer
Deploy a second, embedding model, upload the photos to it in the portal, and compare its vector output with her expected answers

stem: A developer deploys the gpt-4.1-mini model in Foundry with the deployment name photo-helper. Her Python code calls client.responses.create(model="gpt-4.1-mini", ...) with an image input, and the call fails because the deployment can't be found. What should she change?

choices.text: Add a detail setting to the image input, because requests without it are sent to a default deployment that doesn't exist
Point the endpoint at the regional URL of the model provider, because image requests skip the Foundry resource endpoint entirely
Pass the deployment name photo-helper as the model value, because requests are routed to a deployment by the name you gave it
Install a separate Azure Vision image analysis package, because image inputs need a different client library than text prompts

stem: A community forum app sends each uploaded picture to a vision-enabled model in Foundry for a short description. One request with a graphic picture of an injury is rejected, and the prompt filter results show the violence category as filtered. What happened?

choices.text: The system that blocks CAPTCHA images misread the picture, because every rejected image is labelled with the violence category
The image file was too large for the request, and the service reports oversized images as filtered under the violence category
The model ran out of output tokens while describing the picture, and the service reports truncated answers as violence filtering
The deployment's content filter checked the image input, rated its violence severity at or above the threshold, and blocked the request

stem: A team's marketing tool was built a while ago against a dall-e-3 deployment in Azure OpenAI. Image generation calls to that deployment no longer work, and the team can't create a new dall-e-3 deployment either. What should they do?

choices.text: Request a quota increase for the dall-e-3 deployment, because a model that stops responding has exceeded its rate limit
Switch the tool to a vision-enabled GPT chat model and ask it to return a picture, because chat models replace image models
Recreate the dall-e-3 deployment in a different Azure region, where the older image model is still offered for new deployments
Deploy a GPT-image series model such as GPT-image-2 and point the tool at it, because dall-e-3 was retired in March 2026

stem: A student's Python script asks a GPT-image series deployment in Foundry to draw a poster. The call succeeds, and the result is a very long string of letters and digits instead of a picture or a link. What should the script do with the string?

choices.text: Decode the string from base64 into bytes and write the bytes to an image file, such as poster.png, which can then be opened or displayed
Send the string back to the deployment as a new prompt, because the first call returns only a draft code that a second call renders
Open the string as a web address in a browser, because the service returns the image as a link that becomes active after rendering
Paste the string into the Foundry portal's search box, because generated images are stored in the project and found there by code

stem: A design team uses a GPT-image series deployment to explore dozens of poster ideas quickly, then renders the chosen idea for print. Generation is slow during the exploration phase. Which approach fits both phases?

choices.text: Keep the default quality and set the detail level to low on the prompt, which skips the slow parts of image generation
Use the high quality setting while exploring ideas, then lower it for the final print so that the file size stays small
Use the low quality setting while exploring ideas, then generate the chosen design again with the high quality setting
Keep the default quality and add the words "quick draft" to the prompt, which tells the model to use its fastest mode

stem: A marketing designer with no coding experience wants to try prompts for campaign images on an image generation deployment in Foundry, compare the results, and then give a developer a working starting point for the team's app. What should she use?

choices.text: The chat playground with a vision-enabled GPT deployment, where she attaches sample photos and asks the model to send back new campaign images
The images playground for the deployment, where she enters prompts and generates images, then uses View code to get matching Python or cURL samples
An Azure Content Understanding analyzer in Foundry Tools, which she trains on earlier campaign images so that it returns new images to the app
The content filter settings page of the deployment, where she types prompts to preview which images the model would create before any code runs

stem: A warehouse app sends a shelf photo to a vision-enabled model and asks "How many boxes are on this shelf?" to update stock levels automatically. Spot checks show the answers are often off by a few boxes. What is the best explanation and response?

choices.text: The app sent the photo by URL rather than as base64 data, and only base64 images are processed at full accuracy for counting tasks
Vision-enabled models can give approximate counts of objects in images, so exact stock levels need another counting method or a human check
The model's temperature was too low, so raising it lets the model look at the shelf several times and settle on a more exact count
The model counted only the boxes named in the photo's file name, so the app should rename each file to list every box shown on the shelf

stem: A children's book app sends the prompt "a friendly dragon reading a book in a library" to a GPT-image series deployment. The call fails, and the error says the generated image was filtered as a result of the safety system. What does this tell the developer?

choices.text: The deployment ran past its rate limit for images, and the service reports rate limiting to the caller as an image blocked by the safety system
The developer's key lacks permission to generate images, and the safety system returns this message to every caller who isn't authorized
The prompt passed the input checks, but the image the model produced was blocked by output moderation, so adjust the prompt wording and try again
The prompt itself was flagged as harmful before any image was created, so the deployment has been suspended until the team appeals the decision

stem: A school district plans a classroom tool that generates illustrations with a GPT-image series model in Foundry. Which TWO statements about the built-in safety measures are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Photorealistic images of minors are blocked by default unless the customer is granted access
A filtered result still returns the image, with the unsafe regions blurred by the safety system
Any developer can turn content filtering fully off in the deployment settings without approval
Content filtering checks only the text of the prompt and never examines the generated images
Input and output moderation, including content filtering, apply to image generation models

stem: A travel agency has a beach photo it likes and wants a beach ball added in the lower-left corner while the rest of the picture stays as it is. It has a GPT-image series deployment in Foundry. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Generate a separate picture of a beach ball, then ask a vision-enabled chat model to compare it with the photo and merge the two pictures
Send the photo to a vision-enabled chat model and ask it to reply with the same photo after it adds a beach ball in the lower-left corner
Generate a new image from a long prompt that describes every detail of the original photo, and add a beach ball in the lower-left corner
Edit the existing photo: send it with a prompt such as "Add a beach ball in the lower-left corner", optionally with a mask that marks that corner

stem: A café owner tries a GPT-image series model in the Foundry images playground with the prompt "a coffee cup". The results are bland and in random styles, while she wants images that match her café's flat, pastel brand look. What should she change first?

choices.text: Rewrite the prompt to describe both the content and the visual style, such as "flat vector illustration of a latte cup, pastel colors"
Keep the short prompt and change the output format to PNG, because PNG images keep the pastel colors of the brand palette
Keep the short prompt and set the quality to low, because lower quality images come out in a simpler and flatter visual style
Keep the short prompt and raise the number of images to ten, because one of ten random results will match the brand style

stem: Users of a greeting-card app complain that they stare at a blank screen while a GPT-image series deployment generates their card, and some requests time out. Which TWO changes does Microsoft document for reducing the wait? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Make the prompt much longer and more detailed, so the model needs fewer attempts to understand the request and finishes it sooner
Use a lower quality setting or a smaller image size, so each image takes less time to generate before the finished file is returned
Send each request to a vision-enabled chat model first, so that the image generation model receives a picture that is already started
Ask for many more images in each request, so the service prepares spare cards in advance and later users receive one immediately
Stream the image generation request with partial images, so previews appear on screen while the final image is still being generated

stem: A recipe website plans two features in Foundry: one writes a text description of each dish photo that users upload, and the other creates brand-new illustrations for recipe pages from a short text brief. Which model choice fits each feature?

choices.text: A single text embedding model for both, comparing each photo and each brief against vectors of earlier recipes
A single vision-enabled GPT chat model for both, with the detail level set to high for the illustration requests
A GPT-image series model for the photo descriptions, and a vision-enabled GPT chat model for the new illustrations
A vision-enabled GPT chat model for the photo descriptions, and a GPT-image series model for the new illustrations

stem: A startup is planning a new app that captions and tags user photos. A tutorial it found uses the Image Analysis 4.0 API in Azure Vision in Foundry Tools. Which TWO statements should guide the decision? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Image Analysis 3.2 is the long-term replacement, because the retirement applies only to version 4.0 of the API
The retirement covers only the cloud API, so a container deployment of Image Analysis keeps working afterwards
For captions and tags, Microsoft's migration guide points to GPT models in Foundry or Azure Content Understanding
Azure Custom Vision is the long-term successor for tagging, because it has no retirement planned at this time
Image Analysis is deprecated and will be retired on September 25, 2028, after which calls to it will fail

stem: A home-appliance retailer wants a lightweight support app: customers upload a photo of a faulty appliance, ask free-form questions such as "Which part is leaking?", and then ask follow-up questions. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: A GPT-image series model, which redraws the photo with the leaking part highlighted as the answer to each question
The Image Analysis tagging feature, which returns a fixed list of tags that the app shows as the answer to each question
The Face service, which detects human faces in the photo and returns their positions as the answer to each question
A vision-enabled GPT model deployed in Foundry, called with each question and the photo in a multi-part message

stem: A student is writing a short Python script with the OpenAI library that sends a photo and a question to a vision-enabled model deployed in her Foundry resource. Which TWO values must the script provide when it creates the client and sends the request? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The key of a separate Azure Vision resource, because image inputs are billed and processed by the Vision service instead
The name she gave to the model deployment, passed as the model value in the request that carries the photo and question
The key of a separate Azure AI Content Safety resource, because every image request must be checked by the app itself
The ID of the dataset the model was trained on, so the service can match the uploaded photo to similar training images
The endpoint of her Foundry resource, used as the client's base URL, together with a key or Microsoft Entra ID credential

stem: A clinic's Python script uses the Azure Language client library (TextAnalyticsClient). Before feedback text is copied to an analytics team, the script must save a copy in which patient names, phone numbers and email addresses are masked. Which call and result value should the script use?

stem: A product team wants a quick prototype that reads each customer review, sorts it into one of their own five categories (such as "billing" or "delivery"), and writes a one-line English summary even when the review is in German. They have no labeled training data. What should they use?

Azure Language custom text classification, trained on a labeled set of reviews for each of the five categories they defined

Azure Language key phrase extraction, then a lookup table that maps each returned phrase to one of the five categories

stem: A support portal routes tickets by the language that Azure Language detects. The team now wants a ticket sent to a person for checking whenever the service is unsure which language it is written in. The code runs result = client.detect_language([text])[0]. Which value should the check use?

stem: A hospital wants to pull medication names, dosages and diagnoses out of doctors' free-text notes, with each item labeled by its type. It has no labeled training data. Which Azure Language feature fits best?

Text analytics for health, which extracts and labels medical information from unstructured clinical text

Language detection, which returns the language of each note together with a confidence score for it

stem: A team is starting a new text analysis project with Azure Language in Foundry Tools. They want to build on features that Microsoft lists as core capabilities, recommended for new development. Which TWO features should they plan around? (Select TWO)

Text summarization

stem: A developer prompts a deployed GPT model to list the people, organizations and places in each news article. The parser that reads the reply keeps breaking because the wording and layout of the list change between runs. What should the developer do?

Train an Azure Language custom NER model on labeled articles before it can find any people or places
Call Azure Language key phrase extraction, which returns the main concepts of each article as a plain list
Send the same prompt to the model twice and keep only the entities that appear in both of the replies

stem: Before writing any code, an analyst wants to paste a long customer report into Microsoft Foundry, ask a model to summarize it, and then ask follow-up questions that refine the analysis in the same conversation. What should the analyst do?

Deploy a general-purpose model in a Foundry project and try it in the chat playground

stem: A developer can process text either with Azure Language features or with a prompt to a deployed general-purpose model. For which TWO requirements is Azure Language the better choice? (Select TWO)

Translate a review into English and then rewrite it as a friendly reply, both done in the same single request
Sort feedback into categories that a manager invents next week, without labeling any examples or training a model
Return a redacted copy of each message with every detected phone number masked, in the same format on every run
Return a language code and a confidence score between 0 and 1 for each message, ready to store in a database field

stem: A developer wants a web app where users speak a question and hear a spoken answer from a model deployed in their own Foundry project, with as little delay as possible. Which model and API fit best?

Deploy a speech-in, speech-out model such as gpt-realtime and send the audio to that deployment

Azure Speech text to speech with SSML, which reads a set of prepared answers aloud with a chosen neural voice
Azure Speech batch transcription, which processes recorded visitor questions asynchronously and returns transcripts
Azure Speech Voice Live API, which combines recognition, a generative model and speech output with noise suppression

Azure Language language detection run on the raw audio, then set the recognition language to the returned code

Put both voice names at the top of the plain text so that the synthesizer reads alternate lines with each

Write an SSML document with a separate voice element for each speaker's lines and a break element between turns
